title: General unfolding of nonconvex polyhedra
formal:
Does every closed embedded polyhedral surface in \(\mathbb R^3\), including nonconvex surfaces, admit a general nonoverlapping unfolding into one connected planar piece?

Precisely, for every compact connected polyhedral two-dimensional manifold \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) without boundary, do there exist a finite union \(C\) of straight segments on its surface and a continuous injective map
\[f:P\setminus C\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2\]
such that \(P\setminus C\) is connected and \(f\) is a rigid Euclidean placement on each triangle of a finite subdivision of the surface away from the cuts?

Cuts may cross original faces. They have zero width, no area of the surface is discarded, and the whole uncut surface must remain connected. Coincidence between copies of cut-boundary points in the planar closure is allowed; overlap between distinct uncut surface points is not. No restriction to genus zero is imposed.
why: This asks whether nonconvex geometry can obstruct every possible connected planar net even when cuts are unrestricted within faces. Resolving it would identify a fundamental limit of cutting and flattening polyhedral surfaces, and distinguish geometric impossibility from the shortcomings of particular meshing or fabrication algorithms.
status_note: Source-open in TOPP Problem 43 (history through 24 July 2008) and explicitly listed as open in the official description of Demaine’s Spring 2025 MIT Lecture 16. On 16 September 2026, this review checked the foundational finite-cut model, boundary contact and the genus-zero restriction of the orthogonal result. It also checked the published December 2025 refolding paper, whose overlap-allowing definition does not resolve this question. Bounded later-work searches and the authors’ book-update pages revealed no resolution of the specified nonoverlapping target. This records dated explicit openness and limited later review; it is not an exhaustive current-status certification or an independent proof audit of every background theorem.

progress.text: The source records general nonoverlapping unfolding results for convex polyhedra, including the source and star unfoldings.
Bern and coauthors exhibit nonconvex edge-ununfoldable polyhedra and show that crossing faces can enable a general unfolding; they also prove an obstruction for a surface with boundary.
A general unfolding is proved for every genus-zero orthogonal polyhedron, with potentially very fine subdivisions and thin strips.
Demaine’s official MIT lecture description explicitly lists the boundaryless general-unfolding problem as open.
The two-step refolding theorem uses possibly overlapping unfoldings. It therefore leaves the nonoverlap requirement in this card unproved.

importance.reason: A central longstanding question in geometric folding, explicitly highlighted by Demaine as a major open problem. It has a simple global existence target, substantial positive and negative results around its boundary, and a direct conceptual connection to producing three-dimensional surfaces from flat material.

sentences: A general unfolding cuts a polyhedral surface along finitely many segments, including segments through faces.
The goal is one connected planar piece with no overlap of its uncut surface.
The question asks whether every closed embedded polyhedral surface admits such an unfolding, including nonconvex surfaces and surfaces with handles.
Convex surfaces and genus-zero orthogonal polyhedra have positive results, while restrictions to original edges or inputs with boundary have counterexamples.
A 2025 refolding theorem permits overlap and therefore does not settle this nonoverlapping existence question.

definitions:
The input is a compact connected surface \(P\) embedded in ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space. It is the union of finitely many closed nondegenerate straight triangles whose intersections are common edges, common vertices or empty. Each edge belongs to exactly two triangles, and every point of the union has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open disk. The latter condition excludes singular pinched vertices and surfaces connected only at isolated points. Thus \(P\) is a closed polyhedral two-manifold, not a solid volume. Its triangulation is a representation of the surface, rather than a restriction on where cuts may lie.

Coordinates are arbitrary real numbers. Neither convexity nor general position is required. The surface may have handles of any finite genus; genus zero means homeomorphic to a sphere. Faces of an original polygonal description may be subdivided into triangles without changing the geometric surface. Self-intersecting surfaces, overlapping copies of faces and surfaces with an existing boundary are outside this embedded closed-surface model.

A cut set \(C\) is a finite union of closed straight line segments contained in \(P\), with each segment lying in a planar face or triangle after subdividing at any face crossings. Intersections and endpoints of the segments can be added as subdivision vertices. The segments need not be original edges, need not lie on a prescribed grid and may have arbitrary real endpoints. There is no uniform upper bound on their number or on the fineness of a subdivision. Curved cuts with infinitely many bends and infinitely many cuts are not allowed.

The surface is cut along \(C\) by separating its two sides wherever present. Its uncut part is \(P\setminus C\); this set must be nonempty and connected in the surface topology. Because it is an open subset of a two-manifold, this requires genuine surface connectivity. It does not allow two otherwise separate pieces to be joined only at one vertex. The finite cut graph has area zero, so all two-dimensional material remains. Boundary copies of cut points are recovered by taking limits from each side.

A precise finite description of a flattening consists of a subdivision \(K\) of the surface triangulation, with every cut a union of edges of \(K\), and one affine Euclidean isometry \(g_\tau\) from the supporting plane of each triangle \(\tau\in K\) into \(\mathbb R^2\). For every \(x\in\tau\setminus C\), set \(f(x)=g_\tau(x)\). Whenever a point lies on two or more triangles and is not cut, these assignments must agree. The resulting map on \(P\setminus C\) must be continuous and injective. Reflections of individual triangle coordinate frames are permitted in specifying the placements; continuity and injectivity enforce a consistent planar surface across uncut adjacencies.

Being an isometry on each triangle means exactly preserving Euclidean distances within that triangle, and hence its lengths, angles and area. The assembled map preserves the lengths of surface paths. It is not required to preserve the three-dimensional straight-line distance between points in different faces. Nor is the intrinsic distance in a nonconvex planar piece generally the straight-line distance through its missing regions.

Nonoverlap is expressed by injectivity on \(P\setminus C\). Interiors cannot cover one another; two distinct uncut points cannot coincide even if each lies on an uncut triangulation edge. Distinct copies of points along the cuts may touch in the closure of the planar image. Such boundary contacts are not gluing operations and do not establish connectivity that the uncut surface lacks. This is the usual boundary-contact convention explicitly used by Damian, Flatland and O’Rourke. Requiring a positive clearance between every pair of boundary portions would impose a stronger condition.

The planar piece may be nonconvex and may have slits or holes. No additional simple-polygon requirement is imposed beyond the connected nonoverlapping flattening just defined; the foundational paper explicitly discusses this distinction. No disconnected dissection followed by rearrangement or new gluing is allowed. The finite subdivision merely expresses the original surface and the cuts; it does not permit stretching, shrinking, removing positive-area strips or covering a portion of the original surface twice.

The quantifiers are \(\forall P\;\exists C,K,(g_\tau)_{\tau\in K}\), subject to the stated geometric conditions. This is an exact existence question. There is no running-time, coordinate bit-length, bounding-box size, minimum strip width or approximation target. Only the final flattened configuration is required: a continuous collision-free physical motion from the original shape to that configuration is a separate question.

An edge unfolding restricts cuts to the original edges of the given polyhedral description. A general unfolding, the target here, permits additional cuts through faces. A vertex unfolding permits pieces to be connected only at vertices and therefore uses a weaker connectivity requirement. Neither the impossibility of an edge unfolding nor the existence of a vertex unfolding decides the general-unfolding question.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal existence statement for the specified closed embedded polyhedral surfaces. A positive proof must establish finite surface cuts, a connected uncut surface and a compatible collection of exact rigid planar triangle placements whose assembled map is injective on the entire uncut surface. No efficient construction or collision-free unfolding motion is required. A negative proof must give a valid surface in this model and show that every finite permitted cut set and every compatible planar placement fail the connectivity or nonoverlap requirement. Ruling out only original-edge cuts, a particular algorithm or a bounded number of cuts is insufficient. Results for convex surfaces alone, overlapping flattenings, disconnected pieces, or surfaces that already have boundary do not settle the target. A numerical mesh picture or approximate nonoverlap check does not replace the complete proof.

source_formulation.text: TOPP Problem 43 asks whether every closed polyhedron can be cut on its surface and flattened into a single planar piece without overlap. Its distinction between general, edge and vertex unfoldings is retained. The finite-cut model is made explicit from the foundational paper, with the boundary-contact convention of the cited orthogonal-unfolding work.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of TOPP Problem 43, with finite-cut and nonoverlap conventions made explicit

context_blocks.text: The surface of a three-dimensional object can be fabricated from flat material by cutting a planar pattern and joining its boundary as prescribed. The question asks whether arbitrary surface cuts always suffice to produce one connected pattern, even when the desired object is nonconvex. It isolates a geometric existence obstruction before manufacturing constraints or algorithmic efficiency are considered.

Convex polyhedra have general nonoverlapping unfoldings. Nonconvex polyhedra can fail to have any edge unfolding, but this does not answer the present question because new cuts can run through faces. Bern and coauthors give a nonconvex example for which those additional cuts make a difference.

Bern and coauthors also construct a polyhedral surface with boundary that cannot be generally unfolded. This shows why “closed” is an essential input condition. Their discussion of cuts distinguishes connected planar pieces from the extra convention that the result must be a simple polygon.

Damian, Flatland and O’Rourke prove general unfoldability for every genus-zero orthogonal polyhedron, whose edges are parallel to three coordinate axes. Their construction can require very thin strips. TOPP’s abbreviated statement of this progress omits genus zero; the cited theorem does not justify removing that restriction.

The official description of Demaine’s Spring 2025 MIT lecture explicitly retains general unfolding of boundaryless polyhedra as an open question. This is a later dated statement of the same broad geometric problem, rather than a new theorem.

The December 2025 two-step refolding theorem concerns common unfoldings that may overlap in the plane. Its introduction and first footnote state that convention explicitly. Consequently the result does not establish a nonoverlapping general unfolding as required here.

General unfolding and convex edge unfolding ask for different extensions of a known convex result: one expands the permitted input shapes, while the other restricts the allowed cuts. The distinction makes nonconvex edge counterexamples relevant context without turning them into solutions of this card.
